scenarios.title: Too close to the carrier
scenarios.objective: Leave room for a teammate while remaining available.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 has the puck and YOU are only a short step away. Navy3 offers a separate option. Gold1 is ahead. This keep-away activity asks partners to avoid occupying the same small space. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU and Navy2 are close together.

questions.prompt: Which navy player is closest to Navy2?
questions.explanation: YOU are two metres from Navy2 in this illustration; Navy3 is farther away.

questions.prompt: What might extra separation give Navy2?
questions.explanation: Separation can offer room and another angle. It cannot guarantee the next pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into separate space while keeping Navy2 in view.
questions.explanation: The reference opens a different support angle. Several distances could suit the players; no universal spacing is claimed.

questions.prompt: Arrange a spacing check.

options.text: Notice whether you are crowding them

questions.explanation: This is a coaching suggestion. Staying closer can be useful in other states, so re-check the situation.

questions.prompt: Imagine pressure reaches Navy2 and a short outlet is needed. Should YOU always move farther away?

options.text: No, a nearby clear outlet may help

questions.explanation: Useful distance depends on pressure and the available passing route.

questions.prompt: Why is more space not the same as going as far away as possible?
questions.explanation: A useful answer connects room with staying available. The source supports near and far support, not one fixed distance.

questions.prompt: If Navy2 needs a short outlet, what should YOU choose?
questions.explanation: Navy2's pressure and passing range matter. A nearby clear outlet can help more than maximum distance.

questions.prompt: What two relationships should shape your spacing?
questions.explanation: Spacing is useful when it gives the carrier room and responds to pressure. The scene does not establish a universal measured distance.

questions.prompt: Place YOU below Navy2 with Navy3 still in view.
questions.explanation: This gives Navy2 a lower option while keeping YOU separate. A different reachable angle can work.

questions.prompt: How can Navy3 change your support choice?
questions.explanation: Navy3 already offers a lower angle, so YOU do not need to crowd Navy2. Use the carrier's pressure and both support lanes to choose.

scenarios.title: Look beyond the nearest jersey
scenarios.objective: Compare a nearby covered teammate with another support option.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have the puck. Navy2 is nearby, but Gold1 occupies the direct line to Navy2. Navy3 is farther away at another angle; Gold2 is away from that illustrated line. Compare the options before trying a pass. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 sits on that near line.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is nearer YOU?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is the nearby partner on the same line.

questions.prompt: Which direct line is occupied by Gold1?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is between YOU and Navy2.

questions.prompt: What should you compare besides distance?

options.text: Whether a teammate is always closest

questions.explanation: Distance alone does not establish availability.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little to inspect a different passing angle.
questions.explanation: This changes the relationship to both targets. It is exploratory; the final choice still depends on defenders and puck travel.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold2 closes Navy3's line before you pass. What could you do?

options.text: Pass to Navy3 because far is always best

questions.explanation: The suggested preference changes if the visible line closes.

questions.prompt: Why might the farther teammate be worth a look here?
questions.explanation: Navy3 offers a different angle while Gold1 occupies the near line. Do not claim the pass is physically guaranteed.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 reaches the corner first, what should YOU check?

options.text: Who owns the puck now and where Navy2 is

questions.explanation: Gold1's arrival can change ownership. Checking the new owner and Navy2 prevents acting on an old picture.

questions.prompt: After YOU control the puck, what two players can shape the next action?
questions.explanation: Gold1 can pressure the recovery and Navy2 can support. Neither position guarantees a pass or pickup.

questions.prompt: Place YOU between Gold1 and Navy2 after the pickup.
questions.explanation: This keeps the defender in view and connects YOU to Navy2. It is one example recovery relationship.

questions.prompt: Why does the nearest player still need a scan?
questions.explanation: Being nearest helps YOU reach the puck, but Gold1 may contest it and Navy2 may offer support. Ownership and pressure still need checking.

scenarios.title: Receive, then find the next picture
scenarios.objective: Refresh teammate and pressure information after reception.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have just controlled a short pass near the faceoff circle in the defending end. The earlier pass is not animated. Navy2 now waits toward centre ice; Navy3 waits along the boards. Gold1 is closer to YOU than Gold2. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU control the puck after reception.
YOU are near a faceoff circle.
Navy2 and Navy3 occupy different areas.

questions.prompt: Where did YOU receive the puck?

options.text: Inside the gold goal at the +x end

questions.explanation: YOU are at the circle in the defending end centre in the supplied practice picture.

questions.prompt: Which locations are useful to update now?
questions.explanation: Check partners and pressure after reception.

questions.prompt: Arrange one receive-and-read routine.

options.text: Notice the new pressure and support

questions.explanation: This is a simple suggested routine. Experienced players may scan before and during reception too.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little toward centre ice to inspect the support picture.
questions.explanation: This creates a new angle away from the nearer pressure side. It is not a proven escape path.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy3 leaves the boards before your next action. What should change?

options.text: Keep passing to the old spot

questions.explanation: The relevant target is the actual teammate location, not a memorized board mark.

questions.prompt: What did you need to learn again after receiving?
questions.explanation: Describe the current pressure or a teammate location. The earlier pass does not decide the next read.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 turns toward the middle, where should YOU look?

options.text: The carrier and the navy end

questions.explanation: Gold1's direction changes the danger. The carrier and protected end keep the recovery connected to the real play.

questions.prompt: What two players help you read the transition?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is the carrier and Navy2 is the nearby defender/support reference. Together they shape where YOU can help.

questions.prompt: Place YOU nearer the middle behind Gold1.
questions.explanation: This example brings YOU toward the transition and keeps the carrier in front. Another controlled recovery lane can fit.

questions.prompt: Why is a turnover a new scene for the team?
questions.explanation: Gold1 now has the puck, so Navy must defend. The carrier route and Navy2's position replace the old attacking plan.

scenarios.title: Handle the puck beside the boards
scenarios.objective: Notice pressure and nearby inside room while carrying.
scenarios.briefing: YOU control the puck beside the boards in the attacking end. Gold1 faces you from the goalward side. Navy2 offers an inside partner near the faceoff circle. This is a puck-control activity, not a checking drill. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU are close to the boards.
Gold1 is on the goalward side.
Navy2 is farther inside the rink.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is farther from the side boards?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is at y=3, farther inside than YOU at y=10.

questions.prompt: Which two things deserve a look before moving?

options.text: A promise that every route works

questions.explanation: These are the source-supported cues; a safe route is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Explore a little inside space while keeping Navy2 available.
questions.explanation: The reference moves away from the boards and the goalward opponent. Other choices may work; no contact or travel-time result is certified.

questions.prompt: Arrange a careful control check.
questions.explanation: This is one coaching routine, not a forced game answer.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 moves inside instead. Should you keep using the same inside spot?
questions.explanation: The useful space depends on where pressure actually is.

questions.prompt: How do the boards change the room you can use?
questions.explanation: They bound one side of the space. Discuss inside support or another available route without assuming a guaranteed escape.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 passes while you move back, what changes first?

options.text: The puck location you must read

questions.explanation: A pass moves the puck, so YOU must turn your eyes and update the route while staying controlled.

questions.prompt: What two cues help your backward practice?

options.text: A claim that facing proves awareness

questions.explanation: The carrier and support side are visible cues. Facing helps orientation but does not prove what YOU saw.

questions.prompt: Place YOU a little toward Navy2 while facing Gold1.
questions.explanation: This example connects YOU to Navy2's support side and keeps Gold1 ahead. It does not grade backward technique.

questions.prompt: What should an adult listen for in this moving read?
questions.explanation: Listen for the player naming Gold1 and the puck, then Navy2 and the changing lane. The scene supports awareness, not a perfect skating test.

scenarios.title: Pressure before a wall reception
scenarios.objective: Read the pressure side before a planned pass reaches the wall.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 holds the puck and plans a pass to YOU near the boards. Gold1 approaches from the circle side; Navy3 is a second navy option along the wall. This freeze is before the pass, so YOU cannot shoot or carry the puck yet. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck still belongs to Navy2.
Gold1 approaches from the circle side.

questions.prompt: Do YOU control the puck at this freeze?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is still the puck owner; this is before the planned reception.

questions.prompt: What can YOU notice before reception?
questions.explanation: Pressure and support are available information. A future shot is not established.

questions.prompt: Arrange this declared two-stage activity.

options.text: Read while Navy2 has the puck
Receive if the planned pass is made

questions.explanation: The reception is conditional, and the next action depends on the new state.

questions.prompt: Show a slightly different receiving angle near the boards.
questions.explanation: The reference changes the approach angle. It is a suggestion, not proof the pass will arrive.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 comes along the boards instead. What is a useful response?

options.text: Use the old plan without looking

questions.explanation: A different pressure side may call for a different touch or route.

questions.prompt: What can you do before the puck is yours?
questions.explanation: Look, communicate and prepare an available target. A puck action must wait for actual control.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 covers the old return line, what should YOU offer?
questions.explanation: The defender changed the lane after the pass. A new angle can give Navy2 another choice if it stays clear.

questions.prompt: Which two changes matter after the reception?

options.text: Gold1 moved onto the old line

questions.explanation: Navy2 is the new carrier and Gold1 removed the old line. Those facts replace the pre-pass picture.

questions.prompt: Place YOU below Navy2, away from Gold1's old line.
questions.explanation: This creates a lower support angle for Navy2. Another clear support place may work.

questions.prompt: Why is moving after a pass part of the play?
questions.explanation: The puck carrier changed and Gold1 covered the first return. Moving creates another support option for Navy2.
